summary.traveler: Saudi Arabia imposes no general exchange controls. Visitors and residents may bring in and take out any amount of foreign currency, but amounts of SAR 60,000 or more in combined value — including cash, bearer instruments, gold bullion, precious metals, gemstones, and jewellery — must be declared to customs via the ZATCA Declaration App, the authority's website, or at designated customs declaration offices at ports of entry and exit. Declarations above this threshold also require documentation of the origin of the funds.
summary.business: Saudi Arabia maintains an open capital account with no foreign exchange restrictions on capital receipts or payments by residents or non-residents. Businesses may freely hold foreign currency accounts, repatriate profits and investment returns, and conduct transactions in foreign currencies. Exchange business operations require licensing from SAMA under the Rules Regulating Money Changing Business. AML and CFT compliance obligations apply to all financial institutions.

rules.bring_foreign_currency_in: There are no restrictions on the amount of foreign currency that may be brought into Saudi Arabia. However, travellers carrying cash, bearer negotiable instruments, gold bullion, precious metals, gemstones, or jewellery with a combined value of SAR 60,000 or more must declare these items to customs. The declaration must be made electronically via the ZATCA Declaration App or the ZATCA website, and then completed in person at the designated customs declaration office at the port of entry. The threshold is established under Article 23 of the Anti-Money Laundering Law (Royal Decree M/20 dated 5/2/1439H). Travellers must also provide official documentation of ownership and source of funds for declared amounts.
rules.take_foreign_currency_out: There are no restrictions on the amount of foreign currency that may be taken out of Saudi Arabia. The same declaration requirement applies at departure: travellers carrying cash, negotiable instruments, gold bullion, precious metals, gemstones, or jewellery with a combined value of SAR 60,000 or more must declare these items. For departing passengers, the declaration must be made before the check-in counters and prior to entering the departure hall. Items prohibited for export, such as antiquities, must also be declared regardless of value.
rules.cash_declaration_threshold: The declaration threshold in Saudi Arabia is SAR 60,000, applicable to the combined value of cash, bearer negotiable instruments, gold bullion, precious metals, precious stones, and fine jewellery. This applies equally at entry and departure and is established under Article 23 of the Anti-Money Laundering Law. For amounts at or above this threshold, a physical visit to the customs declaration office at the port is mandatory even if an electronic declaration has been submitted in advance. Customs may seize and hold amounts for up to 72 hours pending investigation in cases of non-declaration or suspected money laundering.
rules.resident_holding_rules: Saudi residents may freely open and hold accounts in foreign currencies at Saudi banks. Customers may deposit and withdraw in any available foreign currency; if that currency is not physically available, payments may be made in Saudi riyals. There are no restrictions on the amount of foreign currency that residents may hold, transfer, or convert. The Saudi riyal has been pegged to the US dollar at SAR 3.75 per USD since 1986, providing exchange rate stability. Residents may freely buy, hold, sell, import, and export gold, except gold of 14 karats or less which is subject to separate provisions.
rules.non_resident_rules: Non-residents face no foreign exchange restrictions in Saudi Arabia. They may hold bank accounts in both Saudi riyals and foreign currencies, convert freely between currencies, and repatriate funds without restriction. Non-resident investors may repatriate profits, dividends, and capital. SAMA confirms that Saudi Arabia imposes no foreign exchange restrictions on capital receipts or payments by non-residents, beyond a prohibition on transactions with Israel under applicable Saudi law.
rules.business_invoicing_settlement: Saudi businesses may freely invoice, settle, and hold balances in foreign currencies. There are no mandatory conversion requirements. Exchange business — including the commercial sale and purchase of foreign currencies, currency trading, and import/export of currencies — requires a licence from SAMA under the Rules Regulating Money Changing Business issued by the Minister of Finance. SAMA distinguishes between Class A licences (domestic exchange only) and Class B/C licences (including import/export of currencies). AML and CFT obligations, including Know Your Customer (KYC) and Customer Due Diligence (CDD) requirements, apply to all financial institutions and exchange businesses.
rules.exchange_controls: Saudi Arabia maintains an open capital account and imposes no foreign exchange restrictions on capital receipts or payments by residents or non-residents. The Saudi riyal is pegged to the US dollar at SAR 3.75 per USD since 1986, a rate managed by SAMA (the Saudi Central Bank) through provision of USD to domestic banks. The 2025 IMF Article IV Consultation confirmed the appropriateness of the peg and noted an open capital account. SAMA supervises all financial institutions under the Saudi Central Bank Law (Royal Decree M/36, 2021). AML/CFT compliance and transaction reporting obligations apply, particularly for exchange businesses, but no capital movement restrictions exist.
rules.banking_conversion_practicality: Foreign currency exchange is widely available across Saudi Arabia through SAMA-licensed commercial banks, exchange companies, and money changing businesses. The SARIE Instant Payment System enables 24/7 real-time domestic transfers. ATMs are widely available and accept international cards. Major international banks including ICBC, Deutsche Bank, and J.P. Morgan operate in Saudi Arabia. For high-value exchange transactions — above SAR 100,000 for Saudi citizens or SAR 50,000 for foreign nationals — SAMA requires exchange businesses to apply KYC/CDD procedures and verify that income aligns with profession and declared activity.
